raw_response:
I would try **Flixier** first for the browser-based workflow you described. Its official [MP4 editor instructions](https://flixier.com/tools/video-editor/mp4-editor) explicitly describe importing a YouTube video by pasting its link, cutting away unwanted parts, trimming clips, and downloading the exported result. Its [cutting workflow](https://flixier.com/tools/cut-videos) also includes combining clips. In practice, the intended sequence is: import the link, put the video on the timeline, cut around each section you want to keep, remove the other pieces, arrange the retained clips together, and export the shorter study video. This is a documentation-based recommendation; I have not run an import or export.

The main catch is the [free plan](https://flixier.com/pricing): it currently allows 10 minutes of exported video per month at 720p, with a Flixier watermark. Your question does not prohibit a watermark or specify a minimum resolution, so those restrictions do not automatically rule it out, but they may matter for regular study use. I also found that one older YouTube-specific page redirects to generic editing instructions, although the live MP4 editor page still explicitly advertises YouTube-link imports. Try your actual source link before spending time on a long edit.

**Cutlab** is another browser option. Its [link-import documentation](https://www.cutlab.in/features/import-video-from-link) explicitly supports public YouTube URLs, and its [editor documentation](https://www.cutlab.in/features/online-video-editor) describes trimming, splitting and arranging clips on a timeline before exporting the resulting video. The editor is described as free, with no watermark or sign-up. Its source restrictions are more explicit: private videos, age-restricted videos and videos longer than 30 minutes cannot be fetched, and even a public link may occasionally fail. Export runs in real time with the tab open; the output is MP4 when supported by the browser, otherwise WebM. It is therefore a documented fit for an accessible source within those limits, rather than a promise that every YouTube lecture will import.

If you need the PC fallback, **[WonderFox Free HD Video Converter Factory](https://www.videoconverterfactory.com/free-hd-video-converter/)** is a Windows application with both a YouTube downloader and basic editing. Its [URL guide](https://www.videoconverterfactory.com/tips/youtube-to-mp3.html) shows pasting a YouTube URL into the Downloader, while its [cut-and-join guide](https://www.videoconverterfactory.com/tips/free-video-cutter-joiner.html) documents trimming selected intervals and merging clips in the chosen order. Use the video download option, then bring the downloaded source into the Converter, make the clips you want, merge them, and save the resulting video. These are modules of the same free application. I have not installed or tested it; the relevant guides were updated in 2024 and 2026.

I also examined the free, self-hosted **[Cut/Storm](https://github.com/vorniches/cutstorm)** project. Its README supports YouTube URL import, trimming and MP4 output, but I could not establish the crucial ability to join several arbitrary, separated sections into one gist. It remains an option to investigate, not a confirmed complete recommendation. The one decisive follow-up is whether its current editor supports that selection-and-concatenation operation; an affirmative documented answer would make it a fit, while an explicit lack of support would rule it out for this task.

I would exclude **[Clippingnet's trimmer](https://clippingnet.com/video-trimmer/)** for your stated requirement: its own workflow says a YouTube source produces timestamped share links and an embed instead of a downloadable video.

These findings reflect live documentation observed on 21 November 2026. Most pages are undated, and the dated WonderFox guides are later than your 19 July 2023 question, so this evidence does not establish what was available when the question was originally posted.
